war.line: The whole world is wet with mutual blood; and murder, which in the case of an individual is admitted to be a crime, is called a virtue when it is committed wholesale.

effort.line: All our power is of God; I say, of God.

all.line: An ever-burning Gehenna will burn up the condemned, and a punishment devouring with living flames.

antony.name: Antony the Great
antony.who: The father of the desert monks.
antony.hook: At about eighteen he heard one Gospel verse in church, walked out, and gave away his farm. He spent the next eighty years in the desert, where emperors wrote to him.

portrait.credit: Saint Anthony the Great, 15th to 17th century. Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

laugh.by: as the desert monks remembered it

quiet.by: as the desert monks remembered it
quiet.line: Put no confidence in thine own righteousness, and regret not nor cogitate upon a matter which is past, and be persistent in restraining thy tongue and thy belly.

learning.line: We Christians therefore hold the mystery not in the wisdom of Greek arguments, but in the power of faith richly supplied to us by God through Jesus Christ.

anger.line: And once also the Arians having lyingly asserted that Antony's opinions were the same as theirs, he was displeased and wroth against them.

alone.line: Fishes, if they remain long on dry land, die. And so monks lose their strength if they loiter among you and spend their time with you. Wherefore as fish must hurry to the sea, so must we hasten to the mountain.

nature.line: 'My book, O philosopher,' replied Anthony, 'is the nature of things that are made, and it is present whenever I wish to read the words of God.'

body.line: 'For,' said he, 'the fibre of the soul is then sound when the pleasures of the body are diminished.'

miracles.line: For the working of signs is not ours but the Saviour's work.

mystery.by: as the desert monks remembered it
mystery.line: Abba Joseph saith, "I do not know." And Abba Anthony said unto him, "In truth, Abba Joseph, thou hast found the way to say, 'I do not know.'"

effort.line: Wherefore virtue has need at our hands of willingness alone, since it is in us and is formed from us.

cassian.name: John Cassian
cassian.who: Monk who carried the wisdom of the Egyptian desert to the West.
cassian.hook: After years among the holiest monks of Egypt, he admitted he still lost his temper alone in his cell. At his pen. At his blunt knife. At his flint, when it would not spark.

portrait.credit: Saint John Cassian, miniature in the Sacra Parallela of John of Damascus, 9th century. Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

pairs.augustine: Augustine's followers attacked Cassian's teaching on grace and effort.
pairs.chrysostom: Chrysostom ordained Cassian a deacon in Constantinople.

anger.line: For the end and aim of patience consists, not in being angry with a good reason, but in not being angry at all.

lie.line: But if we prefer what is for another's advantage to our own good, and satisfy the demands of the Apostle, we shall certainly have to put up with the necessity of lying.

body.line: For excess of fasting and gluttony come to the same thing, and an unlimited continuance of vigils is equally injurious to a monk as the torpor of a deep sleep.

deeper.line: But as the renewal of our soul grows by means of this study, Scripture also will begin to put on a new face, and the beauty of the holier meanings will somehow grow with our growth.

isaac.name: Isaac the Syrian
isaac.who: Hermit and bishop, read by monks East and West to this day.
isaac.hook: Made bishop of Nineveh, he quit after five months. He wrote that a merciful heart burns with love for every creature, even the demons.

portrait.credit: Isaac Sirin miniature, Ioasaf Khokholek, scribe of the Kirillo-Belozersky monastery, 1518. Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

laugh.line: Be not friends with one that loves laughter and derision.

quiet.line: Love silence above all things. It brings thee near the fruit which the tongue is too weak to interpret.

anger.line: A zealous man will never reach peace of mind. And he that is destitute of peace is also destitute of gladness. Peace of mind is called complete health, zeal is the contrary of peace.

alone.line: Love the ease of solitude rather than satisfying the hunger of the world and the converting of the multitude of heathen peoples from error unto adoring God.

tell.line: Spread thy mantle over the sinner and cover him.

nature.line: The first book given by God to the rational beings, is the nature of the created things. Written teachings have been added only after aberration.

body.line: The knowledge of God does not dwell in a body that loves comfort.

mystery.line: By faith we are instructed about those unattainable things, not by investigation and the power of knowledge.

effort.line: For the help of God is necessary for deliverance. When he knows that he needs divine help, he will frequently pray. And by much beseeching the heart becomes humble.

all.line: The retribution of the sinners is this, that He repays them with resurrection instead of with justice.

macrina.name: Macrina the Younger
macrina.who: Eldest sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa. Gregory called her the Teacher.
macrina.hook: When her fiancé died, she refused every other suitor. Then she talked her proud brother Basil out of his vanity, and her rich mother into sharing the servants' bread.

portrait.credit: St. Macrina the Younger, fresco in Saint Sophia Cathedral, Kyiv, 11th century. Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

pairs.nyssa: Macrina was Gregory of Nyssa's older sister. He wrote down her words.

learning.by: as her brother Gregory recorded her words

anger.by: as her brother Gregory recorded her words
anger.line: But, whenever their impulse is towards what is noble, then they become matter for praise, as his desire did to Daniel, and his anger to Phineas, and their grief to those who nobly mourn.

tell.by: as her brother Gregory remembered it
tell.line: Will you not cease to be insensible to the divine blessings? Will you not remedy the ingratitude of your soul?

tears.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
tears.by: as her brother Gregory tells it
tears.line: She quoted the Apostle's words about the duty of not being grieved for them that sleep; because only men without hope have such feelings.

calm.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
calm.by: as her brother Gregory recorded her words
calm.line: It will therefore be no detriment to our participation in the Good, that the soul should be free from such emotions.

mystery.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
mystery.by: as her brother Gregory recorded her words

deeper.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
deeper.by: as her brother Gregory recorded her words
deeper.line: It is impossible to make the framework of the narrative correspond with the truth, if we understand it literally; we can do that only by translating each detail into an equivalent in the world of ideas.

all.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
all.by: as her brother Gregory recorded her words
all.line: But He that becomes all things will be in all things too; and herein it appears to me that Scripture teaches the complete annihilation of evil.

justin.name: Justin Martyr
justin.who: Philosopher who became the first great defender of the faith.
justin.hook: He shopped around for a philosophy and walked out on a teacher who asked to be paid. A stranger by the sea talked him into Christ.

portrait.credit: Saint Justin the Philosopher, Theophanes the Cretan, 1545-1546. Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

pairs.irenaeus: Irenaeus read Justin and quotes him.

learning.line: Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians.

dreams.line: For the prophetical gifts remain with us, even to the present time.

miracles.line: For numberless demoniacs throughout the whole world, and in your city, many of our Christian men exorcising them in the name of Jesus Christ, Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, have healed and do heal.

mystery.line: Philosophy is, in fact, the greatest possession, and most honourable before God, to Whom it leads us and alone commends us.

war.line: We who formerly used to murder one another do not only now refrain from making war upon our enemies.

irenaeus.name: Irenaeus of Lyons
irenaeus.who: Bishop of Lyons. As a boy he heard Polycarp, who had known the apostle John.
irenaeus.hook: To mock one sect's grand names for hidden cosmic powers, he invented his own: the Gourd, Utter-Emptiness, the Cucumber and the Melon.

portrait.credit: Saint Irenaeus, stained-glass window, Lucien Bégule, 1901. Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

pairs.justin: Irenaeus read Justin and quotes him.

rich.line: For whatsoever we acquired from unrighteousness when we were heathen, we are proved righteous, when we have become believers, by applying it to the Lord's advantage.

body.line: Here he manifestly declares the body to be the temple in which the Spirit dwells.

dreams.line: Others have foreknowledge of things to come: they see visions, and utter prophetic expressions.

miracles.line: Others still, heal the sick by laying their hands upon them, and they are made whole.

mystery.line: We are able by the grace of God to explain some of them, while we must leave others in the hands of God.

all.line: Thus also the punishment of those who do not believe the Word of God, and despise His advent, and are turned away backwards, is increased; being not merely temporal, but rendered also eternal.

martin.name: Martin of Tours
martin.who: Soldier turned monk and bishop, the best loved saint of Gaul.
martin.hook: As a young cavalryman he cut his cloak in half with his sword for a freezing beggar. Later he told his commander, the future emperor Julian, that he was Christ's soldier and could not fight.

portrait.credit: Saint Martin and the Beggar, El Greco, 1597-1599. Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

laugh.by: as Sulpicius Severus, who knew him, recorded it
laugh.line: No one ever saw him enraged, or excited, or lamenting, or laughing.

alone.by: as Sulpicius Severus, who knew him, recorded it
alone.line: Martin was accustomed to say to you, that such an abundance of power was by no means granted him while he was a bishop, as he remembered to have possessed before he obtained that office.

calm.by: as Sulpicius Severus, who knew him, recorded it
calm.line: No one ever saw him enraged, or excited, or lamenting, or laughing; he was always one and the same: displaying a kind of heavenly happiness in his countenance, he seemed to have passed the ordinary limits of human nature.

body.by: as Sulpicius Severus, who knew him, recorded it
body.line: It is not fitting that a Christian should die except among ashes; and I have sinned if I leave you a different example.

war.line: I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.

benedict.name: Benedict of Nursia
benedict.who: Author of the Rule that has shaped Western monks for fifteen hundred years.
benedict.hook: As a young man he lived three years in a cave. A friend lowered bread to him on a rope, with a little bell tied to it.

portrait.credit: Saint Benedict, Hans Memling, 1487. Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

pairs.gregory: Gregory the Great wrote the only early life of Benedict.

laugh.line: But as for buffoonery or idle words, such as move to laughter, we utterly condemn them in every place, nor do we allow the disciple to open his mouth in such discourse.

quiet.line: The ninth degree of humility is that a monk restrain his tongue from speaking; and, keeping silence, do not speak until he is spoken to.

learning.by: as Gregory the Great recorded it

tell.line: Let him not shut his eyes to the faults of offenders; but as soon as they appear, let him strive with all his might to root them out.

effort.line: If he sees some good in himself, let him credit it to God, not to himself. But let him know that evil is always his own doing, and count it as his own.

boethius.name: Boethius
boethius.who: Philosopher and the top civil servant of Gothic Italy.
boethius.hook: Condemned without a hearing, he wrote a book in his cell while he waited to die. In it, Philosophy walks in and throws out the Muses of self-pity.

portrait.credit: Boethius teaching his students, 1385. Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

learning.line: Examine carefully what I have said, and if possible, reconcile faith and reason.

anger.line: Pity is rather due to the criminal, who ought to be brought to the judgment-seat by his accusers in a spirit not of anger, but of compassion and kindness.

calm.line: Joy, hope and fear Suffer not near, Drive grief away: Shackled and blind And lost is the mind Where these have sway.

mystery.line: I have long pondered this problem with such mind as I have and all the light that God has lent me.

effort.line: Therefore, withstand vice, practise virtue, lift up your souls to right hopes, offer humble prayers to Heaven.
